claims.claim: Reviewers state that the tutorials fail to provide useful explanations for advanced or basic mechanics, requiring players to rely on external wikis or guides.

citations.review_text: I came over from Satisfactory, to which I'm biased to, but the controls and interface definitely take some time to getting used to. The tutorial is very weak in terms of explaining how to perform some basic functions. However, overall the game is fun and if you like high level macro games (https://youtu.be/NgHvdCcmQ4o), you'll love this game.

I really don't enjoy games which pretty much require you to go to the web to figure aspects of them out, it just spoils the fun. It's crazy that they spend time programming a good game, but fail to have useful information in much of their tutorials (how to use combinators, deciders...even the idea of red and green wires and blueprints just appear following research without explanations).

You develop all sorts of technologies, but within a few hours the technologies, and how to use them, become non-intuitive. 

Satisfactory managed these technology steps almost seemlessly, and in a 3-D world. Factorio's 2D nature makes it feel like it's a 1980's version of Satisfactory.

In short, go and complete Satisfactory first, and if like me you've done that, then consider Factorio.

citations.review_text:
One of the best games I've played. Do NOT let the 2D aspect turn you away. I was initially offput by having a factory game in 2D (especially after Satisfactory was my introductory game to factory games) and I wasn't the biggest fan of the graphics, but this game ended up being one of the best games out there.

If you have no experience in automation games, this one can be pretty brutal to start with. I would probably recommend starting with Satisfactory. I tried this game first, got lost even in the tutorial, and put it down for a long time. After understanding the concept of the game better from Satisfactory, the tutorial felt much more approachable because I then understood the flow of the game and the purpose of everything.

There are ways to get around the 2D aspect with things like railways that are lifted higher off the ground or belts that go underground. These help a lot. The game is highly optimized so extremely large factories are possible without performance issues.

Mods are built into the client and very easy to download and update.

Resource patches are of limited quantity. Personally, that gives me a lot of anxiety, especially with the enemies. I'm really not a big fan of having to ration everything in an automation game. I just want to build large systems and fight bugs. Thankfully, there's a mod for that! If you're like me, get an infinite resource mod to make the game a little more chill. If you like the challenge of rationing resources, you can do that too! Resource patches are plentiful, don't get me wrong. You can get a ton of resources from one patch, but it's really just the fact that it's limited that gets me anxious.

This game also never goes on sale. The devs have made a stand against that. But the game is well worth the full price. The DLC also adds at least 4-5x playtime per run. Highly recommend Space Age.

THE factory game, (I bought it before it arrived on steam and took a long while to grab a steam key so my playtime is much higher than shown).

Best modding support I've ever encountered, it will track mods on a per-save bases and manedge updating, ordering and, dependencies more smoothly than any other game (only nitpick being that you have to go to the game's website to see what a mod's dependents are as the in-game interface only shows what mods a selected mod's depends on not the inverse).

claims.claim: Map and mineral resource deposits are randomly generated on each playthrough.

citations.review_text:
I haven't finished the game yet, I'm still working my way through the Space Age expansion, but I've been enjoying it so much that I felt the need to write a review before even reaching the end. I'm making good progress, and every new challenge has only made me appreciate the game even more.

I come from Satisfactory, so my brain is naturally wired to chase perfect ratios and maximum efficiency. Factorio absolutely lets you play that way, but it also feels like it has far greater potential for scaling. The ability to grow your factory and mass-produce on an enormous scale is on another level. Another big advantage is that the map and mineral resource deposits are randomly generated, so every playthrough changes the way you design and build your factory. In Satisfactory, resource nodes are always in fixed locations, which eventually leads players to discover and build in the same "perfect" base locations.

The possibilities are practically endless. Factorio is, in my opinion, the pinnacle of factory-building games. It gives you an incredible amount of freedom and is the ultimate sandbox for anyone who enjoys automation. Eventually, your factory becomes multiplanetary, you're automating production across different planets, with logistics systems constantly sending and receiving resources to keep everything running. It's an amazing feeling when it all comes together.

I understand why the game can feel intimidating. It's complex, and there's definitely a learning curve. But one of Factorio's biggest strengths is how easy it is to rebuild and improve your factory. The blueprint system is incredibly powerful compared to Satisfactory. It lets you copy, move, replace, and scale entire sections of your factory in seconds. Because of that, you should never be afraid to experiment, make mistakes, and redesign things as you learn.

Factorio is a masterpiece in its genre, and with version 2.1 just around the corner, I think anyone with even a slight interest in factory-b…

This is a game you can pick up again and again. 
Unlike many other factorio games (this game kinda started the genre). Factorio manages to keep goals clear without dictating your way, but still pushing you without feeling pushed towards the next goal. 

It also lets you shape the world in your image, you get to choose and build something that is entirely yours to be! 

It is very intuitive(Apart from the more complex circuit logic, which is 100% optimal and not at all required to finish the game), and the quality of life updates they added over the years has made this game easier and easier to get into. 

I found that this game is something you will come back to, and every playthrough is a new story.
With Space Age, the game also exploded in possibilities, no longer do you need to limit yourself to the original planet, but with Space Age you get to enjoy new game changing systems, that totally revamp how some particular thing works. 

I can never recommend this game enough!

So, you've seen the overwhelmingly positive reviews, and you're still on the fence. Maybe it's the art style, or maybe you aren't sure this is the kind of game you're looking for.

I'm here to tell you to take a leap of faith. 

This is the kind of game that takes a minute to click, but once it does, you can't put it down. The other reviews and jokes about how addicting this game is are not exaggerated. It takes problem solving, an inherently dopamine-inducing task, and gamifies it, turning it into short repeatable loops almost. If you're a programmer, it takes what you love about programming and makes it into a game. If you aren't a programmer, this game will make you wonder why you aren't one (AI crisis not withstanding).

The art will grow on you if it hasn't already. The soundtrack is impeccable. The quality of life this game provides is the gold standard, I've never seen another game do better QoL than this one. The modding is done with ease through the Steam Workshop, integrated directly into the game, and is one of the best modding scenes I've seen (amongst Minecraft and Project Zomboid). The DLC, while priced the same as the game, actually feels like an extension of the game, and offers tons of hours of content. 

All in all, buy it. You will not regret it. The only regret I can confidently say I have about this game is that I wish I had more time to play it.

Lets be real, I have been playing this game a week or two every few years for 10 years. I love this game, it is great. 

I am/was literally a scientist for work and still this game challenges me in ways I don't expect. Something about learning to make your first factory, then realizing you need to scrap parts of it to make a better or more efficient or just less bad version is very satisfying. You really get a sense of your progress in organization and optimization.

I bought Space Age without even ever getting to the stage in the game where that would even open up lol, because I am determined now. I play this on my Macbook Air M3, and it never ceases to amaze me how seamlessly it plays on MacOS. To have an internal mod section that works on MacOS too is such a great quality of life enhancement. To know I played this as a man in my twenties with a custom built Desktop Tower all the way into my 30s with a general laptop is just wild to me.

I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys organization, factory games, progression systems, and problem solving. Sometimes it feels like work, but for those of us who love using our minds for these types of things it is easily the best game of it's genre even to this day. I prefer it over Satisfactory, due to the isometric view.

claims.claim: The game includes a free demo version allowing players to experience the gameplay before purchasing.

citations.review_text:
13 years after first Early Access release and 6 years after the official release, and the game is still getting continuous updates and improvements.

I don't know of any player who has enjoyed the game and spent less than 300 hours on it.
It is one of those comfort games that I keep coming back to over and over again.

This is the game for you if you like:
* Automation
* Iterative design and improvements
* Complex logic
* Trains and advanced logistics
* Sandbox-style make-your-own-difficulty
* Community
* Mod support (as in the game is designed to be modded to your own liking)

And if you remain unsure if you'll like it, the free demo is a very limited version of the full game but gives the full experience still. It costs you nothing but time to try it out.
Fair warning: If you enjoy the game, it will cost you a LOT of time!

I'll be honest, Space age is very much for people that have completed the game and it detracts somewhat from the overall experience of new players. 
But this IS the grand daddy of the genre. 
Space age has a learning curve of here is a cliff <shove> too bad too sad if you aren't ready.
I'd recommend dyson sphere project and satisfactory over this for more casual players but there is a demo, and you will know what you are in for by the end of the demo. If you like creating huge bases of sprawling factories turing one component into another this game is for you. 
What it does very well is that you are constantly unlocking new <things> that change how you need to build out your base, 
My kids call it spreadsheet games. But there is a reason I'm still playing years after getting it ,am over 500 hours in and haven't finished the expansion. 
Over all highly positive but if you do end up in a corner and feel like it is just a grind, step back and look at what you are doing. The game will not hold your hand and will let you make mistakes that feel like you want to throw the game away. 
....And yet there is a gem that scratches an itch that can't be found in many clones that came after it.
You will need to look up a guide at some point and that is ok (eg nuclear power ratios) but it is a game that lets you build to a scale that most don't and it doesn't feel like you were robbed or forced to pay to win (there is no pay to win) 20,000,000 green chips is an achievment, and you aren't making these in lots of 10.
You'll think the game sucks and then realise there are tools you unlocked that you ignored that make your current issue easy again. 
It will not hold your hand

citations.review_text: I don't need to praise Factorio's excellent game design decisions or how satisfying growing the factory is. Wube knew what they wanted to create and made pretty much only good decisions when developing it further. What isn't praised enough is the excellent optimisation and the best controller control scheme I've ever seen in a game like this, making playing it on the Steam Deck a pleasure, both on the go and on the TV from the couch whenever I prefer that over sitting at my desk.

Amazing game and amazing ongoing work by the Devs to keep improving it. I have several hundred hours in the base game and am also loving the Space Age expansion/DLC. User interface is great, so many design elements are well thought out. Designing and tweaking manufacturing builds is super satisfying. Game also works great on Steam Deck. A true masterpiece!

citations.review_text:
The Factory must grow.

Overall after 350 hours I can definitely recommend it, althought there are a few aspects where I believe Factorio didn't reach it's full potential or developers couldn't find enough time to add more depth.

Generally - it's a spreadsheet game like EVE Online and similar to it. The main appeal of the game (at least for me) is not the fight with biters, not planet exploration, but optimization. How well can you structure the base. How well can you solve ratio problems, belt configurations, train system (honestly, figuring out how train signals work in this game without any guides or tips feels like discovering who Zodiac killer is on your own), mini-extraction colonies defense, etc. It's basically a giant puzzle-optimization game.
After you finish the main game and would like more - play Space Exploration. You won't regret it.

The good: 
- Game is massive. As in there is a lot to do and find what exactly to your taste (deathworld or peaceful settings, or no biters at all; being a spaghetti belter or ADHD-optimization fiend;) and it is further pushed by some achievements (finish game under X hours, building no more than X items by hand, not using drones, etc.).
It took me around 55-60 hours to finish the game for the first time. And it wasn't a chore, it was a race with myself and it felt really incredible to see that rocket go off to space for the first time.
- The whole automation and verticle-horizontal scaling just tickles that specific engineer itch in my brain, same way my work does. There is no hand-holding how to do things. There is also no "correct" way to do things. Pretty much any approach has it's right and scenario to exist. Just watching how other people solve same issues, how they structure their bases, what they focus on, etc. - is incredibly interesting on it's own.
- Mods. My god, this community is one of the most amazing ones in terms of mods. Almost anything that you can think of - you can find in mods. Things that trick you…

[h1]I don't think that anyone reading a review should play Factorio.[/h1]
At this point, especially given the game's popularity, if you don't already know if Factorio is going to be for you or not, then it probably isn't. I can imagine someone getting recommended this game but then discovering that it's a complete slog for them.

And I'm going to try and articulate why.

[h3]Learning Curve? What's that?[/h3]
There's a lot of brick walls of apparent complexity that can feel incredibly daunting when you first arrive at them, and I would surmise that a large majority of people who didn't enjoy Factorio came to that conclusion at one of those moments. It's pretty common knowledge among most Factorio players that chemical science, with it's brand new buildings and fluids and oil processing and whatnot, is the first major hurdle to getting [i]invested[/i] in Factorio. I don't know how much the tutorial has advanced since the game's earlier days, but I don't even think a good tutorial would make it any more approachable.

The annoying thing is that, in isolation, nothing in Factorio is [i]that[/i] hard to understand. On the surface level, there's no singular mechanic that causes players grief. However, the amalgamation of all the systems coming together is what makes the game the beast that it can become. The biggest example I can point to of that are the ratios of inputs/outputs. There are very few [i]intuitive[/i] ratios in this game. It's not easy 1:2 or 3:4 ratios across the board, and even once you understand these ratios, there's dozens of possible bottlenecks that you have to iterate over to find any problems that come up in your factory, which can start to feel overwhelming fairly quickly.

As I play and see other games that were inspired by Factorio, they do far, far better jobs not only introducing players to their mechanics, but also making those mechanics themselves interact in a cleaner way. Shapez 2 comes to mind as a game that took everything that'…

[h1]I don't think that anyone reading a review should play Factorio.[/h1]
At this point, especially given the game's popularity, if you don't already know if Factorio is going to be for you or not, then it probably isn't. I can imagine someone getting recommended this game but then discovering that it's a complete slog for them.

And I'm going to try and articulate why.

[h3]Learning Curve? What's that?[/h3]
There's a lot of brick walls of apparent complexity that can feel incredibly daunting when you first arrive at them, and I would surmise that a large majority of people who didn't enjoy Factorio came to that conclusion at one of those moments. It's pretty common knowledge among most Factorio players that chemical science, with it's brand new buildings and fluids and oil processing and whatnot, is the first major hurdle to getting [i]invested[/i] in Factorio. I don't know how much the tutorial has advanced since the game's earlier days, but I don't even think a good tutorial would make it any more approachable.

The annoying thing is that, in isolation, nothing in Factorio is [i]that[/i] hard to understand. On the surface level, there's no singular mechanic that causes players grief. However, the amalgamation of all the systems coming together is what makes the game the beast that it can become. The biggest example I can point to of that are the ratios of inputs/outputs. There are very few [i]intuitive[/i] ratios in this game. It's not easy 1:2 or 3:4 ratios across the board, and even once you understand these ratios, there's dozens of possible bottlenecks that you have to iterate over to find any problems that come up in your factory, which can start to feel overwhelming fairly quickly.

As I play and see other games that were inspired by Factorio, they do far, far better jobs not only introducing players to their mechanics, but also making those mechanics themselves interact in a cleaner way. Shapez 2 comes to mind as a game that took everything that'…

I'll be honest, Space age is very much for people that have completed the game and it detracts somewhat from the overall experience of new players. 
But this IS the grand daddy of the genre. 
Space age has a learning curve of here is a cliff <shove> too bad too sad if you aren't ready.
I'd recommend dyson sphere project and satisfactory over this for more casual players but there is a demo, and you will know what you are in for by the end of the demo. If you like creating huge bases of sprawling factories turing one component into another this game is for you. 
What it does very well is that you are constantly unlocking new <things> that change how you need to build out your base, 
My kids call it spreadsheet games. But there is a reason I'm still playing years after getting it ,am over 500 hours in and haven't finished the expansion. 
Over all highly positive but if you do end up in a corner and feel like it is just a grind, step back and look at what you are doing. The game will not hold your hand and will let you make mistakes that feel like you want to throw the game away. 
....And yet there is a gem that scratches an itch that can't be found in many clones that came after it.
You will need to look up a guide at some point and that is ok (eg nuclear power ratios) but it is a game that lets you build to a scale that most don't and it doesn't feel like you were robbed or forced to pay to win (there is no pay to win) 20,000,000 green chips is an achievment, and you aren't making these in lots of 10.
You'll think the game sucks and then realise there are tools you unlocked that you ignored that make your current issue easy again. 
It will not hold your hand

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game features a steep learning curve and can be overwhelming to learn for players new to the genre or automation systems.

citations.review_text:
One of the best games I've played. Do NOT let the 2D aspect turn you away. I was initially offput by having a factory game in 2D (especially after Satisfactory was my introductory game to factory games) and I wasn't the biggest fan of the graphics, but this game ended up being one of the best games out there.

If you have no experience in automation games, this one can be pretty brutal to start with. I would probably recommend starting with Satisfactory. I tried this game first, got lost even in the tutorial, and put it down for a long time. After understanding the concept of the game better from Satisfactory, the tutorial felt much more approachable because I then understood the flow of the game and the purpose of everything.

There are ways to get around the 2D aspect with things like railways that are lifted higher off the ground or belts that go underground. These help a lot. The game is highly optimized so extremely large factories are possible without performance issues.

Mods are built into the client and very easy to download and update.

Resource patches are of limited quantity. Personally, that gives me a lot of anxiety, especially with the enemies. I'm really not a big fan of having to ration everything in an automation game. I just want to build large systems and fight bugs. Thankfully, there's a mod for that! If you're like me, get an infinite resource mod to make the game a little more chill. If you like the challenge of rationing resources, you can do that too! Resource patches are plentiful, don't get me wrong. You can get a ton of resources from one patch, but it's really just the fact that it's limited that gets me anxious.

This game also never goes on sale. The devs have made a stand against that. But the game is well worth the full price. The DLC also adds at least 4-5x playtime per run. Highly recommend Space Age.

Do you love games that you can optimize with spreadsheets? Games where you can "program" your own custom creations? You'll love this game.

Beating it doesn't require you get full into the weeds. Fair warning many ppl find the depth and complexity overwelming but if you can push through that then it's well worth your time.

I haven't finished the game yet, I'm still working my way through the Space Age expansion, but I've been enjoying it so much that I felt the need to write a review before even reaching the end. I'm making good progress, and every new challenge has only made me appreciate the game even more.

I come from Satisfactory, so my brain is naturally wired to chase perfect ratios and maximum efficiency. Factorio absolutely lets you play that way, but it also feels like it has far greater potential for scaling. The ability to grow your factory and mass-produce on an enormous scale is on another level. Another big advantage is that the map and mineral resource deposits are randomly generated, so every playthrough changes the way you design and build your factory. In Satisfactory, resource nodes are always in fixed locations, which eventually leads players to discover and build in the same "perfect" base locations.

The possibilities are practically endless. Factorio is, in my opinion, the pinnacle of factory-building games. It gives you an incredible amount of freedom and is the ultimate sandbox for anyone who enjoys automation. Eventually, your factory becomes multiplanetary, you're automating production across different planets, with logistics systems constantly sending and receiving resources to keep everything running. It's an amazing feeling when it all comes together.

I understand why the game can feel intimidating. It's complex, and there's definitely a learning curve. But one of Factorio's biggest strengths is how easy it is to rebuild and improve your factory. The blueprint system is incredibly powerful compared to Satisfactory. It lets you copy, move, replace, and scale entire sections of your factory in seconds. Because of that, you should never be afraid to experiment, make mistakes, and redesign things as you learn.

Factorio is a masterpiece in its genre, and with version 2.1 just around the corner, I think anyone with even a slight interest in factory-b…

The best automation/industrial game bar none. It is extremely optimized and runs on my mid-spec (low-end GPU) laptop. I recommend doing the first playthrough without the dlc nor guides, and a second run with the dlc. Amazing mod support and integration, without requiring external programs.

claims.claim: The game operates natively on Linux and MacOS systems with stable performance and lack of technical issues.

citations.review_text: Tons of content, works natively on Linux systems with nearly 0 problems, good modding community. Im 300 hours in with the dlc and there’s still plenty of things i wanna do. Overall a solid game, i like it but if I’d known about the kovarex's distasteful pricing [i]"philosophy"[/i] I wouldn't have spent a dime on it from the start

Lets be real, I have been playing this game a week or two every few years for 10 years. I love this game, it is great. 

I am/was literally a scientist for work and still this game challenges me in ways I don't expect. Something about learning to make your first factory, then realizing you need to scrap parts of it to make a better or more efficient or just less bad version is very satisfying. You really get a sense of your progress in organization and optimization.

I bought Space Age without even ever getting to the stage in the game where that would even open up lol, because I am determined now. I play this on my Macbook Air M3, and it never ceases to amaze me how seamlessly it plays on MacOS. To have an internal mod section that works on MacOS too is such a great quality of life enhancement. To know I played this as a man in my twenties with a custom built Desktop Tower all the way into my 30s with a general laptop is just wild to me.

I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys organization, factory games, progression systems, and problem solving. Sometimes it feels like work, but for those of us who love using our minds for these types of things it is easily the best game of it's genre even to this day. I prefer it over Satisfactory, due to the isometric view.

claims.claim: The developers maintain a policy of never putting the game on sale.

citations.review_text:
I tried avoiding this game despite liking automation games. Mostly because Factorio is never on sale. 

I would not recommend this game as a first time automation game...Despite it being the first automation game. That nomination would go to Satisfactory.

Those qualifiers aside, I enjoyed this game much more than I expected. Factorio is good, but space age expansion makes it so much better.

The ultimate automation game. Every other automation game just gives me the itch to play Factorio. It can be really overwhelming to learn and takes a certain mindset to play. Patience is more than virtue in Factorio. If you like automation games, solving puzzles, weapons of mass destruction, space travel, trains, mass genocide, or all of the above - get this game. Don't worry about waiting for a sale either, there won't be one!
